for_students:
Your Career Compass is a starting point, not a final answer. It shows which kinds of work tend to energise you, based on your interests right now, and interests grow and shift as you try new things. Use it to explore, not to box yourself in.

Start by reading the careers listed under your top letters and marking three that make you curious. Then do some real-world research: watch a day-in-the-life video, message a senior from your school who studies that field, or ask a cousin in that profession what their week actually looks like. Check entry routes early, because admission tests, licensing rules and subject requirements differ by country, and many start with the subjects you choose at 15 or 16.

You have probably heard the doctor-engineer-lawyer speech at least once, maybe over dinner with the whole family listening. Those are good careers, but they are not the only good ones. A degree is one route; apprenticeships, certifications, bootcamps, portfolios and remote freelancing are others, and in 2026 many employers care about what you can do as much as where you studied.

Finally, talk to your parents with your results in hand. If they moved countries, worked long hours or gave up their own plans so you could have choices, it makes sense that they worry. Share what excites you, listen properly to their concerns, and look for paths that honour both your interests and your family's hopes.
for_parents:
Your child's Career Compass is a window into what naturally interests and motivates them. It is not a verdict, and it does not replace your guidance. Used respectfully, it can turn a tense conversation about the future into a shared exploration.

Read the report together and ask open questions: 'Which of these surprised you?' 'What would a good working day look like for you?' Listen more than you speak. Many parents find their child's interests fit more fields than they expected; a child who loves helping people may thrive in medicine, but also in psychology, nursing, teaching or physiotherapy.

Many desi parents made real sacrifices, sometimes moving countries and starting again from zero, so their children could have security. Wanting a 'safe' career for your child is love, not control. Still, try not to push a field only because of 'log kya kahenge', relatives' opinions or what was prestigious a generation ago. The 2026 job market rewards skills, adaptability and genuine interest, and a motivated student in a less famous field often outperforms an unhappy one in a 'safe' field.

Be honest about practical realities such as fees, visas, distance from home and family responsibilities, and share your own experience of work. Above all, your support matters more than any test. A child who feels trusted to choose, and knows their parents stand behind them, has the strongest possible start.

faq.q: My parents want me to be a doctor, but my results say otherwise. What should I do?
faq.a: First, don't use the report as a weapon in an argument. Share it calmly and explain what excites you and why. Ask what your parents hope medicine will give you: security, respect, a life of service? Then show them careers that offer the same things, such as pharmacy, psychology, biomedical engineering or data work in healthcare. If you're genuinely unsure, spend a few weeks shadowing a doctor, volunteering in a hospital or trying medical entrance practice papers, and see how it feels. A respectful, informed conversation usually works far better than a standoff.

faq.q: My top code doesn't match the subjects I'm already taking. Is it too late?
faq.a: Not at all. Most interest areas connect with several subject combinations. A Maths and Physics student with a strong Artistic score can move into architecture, UI/UX design or game development, while a Biology and Chemistry student with a strong Enterprising score might enjoy healthcare management or pharma marketing. Many universities accept students from different subject backgrounds into business, social science, media and computing degrees, sometimes with a foundation year or bridging course. Look for the overlap rather than starting from scratch.

faq.q: Can I build a career through freelancing without a university degree?
faq.a: Yes, and many young desis already do, from Dhaka to Dallas, especially in design, writing, video editing, development, digital marketing and bookkeeping. Free or low-cost online courses can get you started. Build a portfolio, begin with small projects and collect good reviews. That said, a degree still helps for visas, government jobs, regulated professions and some corporate roles, so many people combine freelancing with a part-time or online degree.

faq.q: How accurate is the Career Compass?
faq.a: It reflects your interests based on your answers today, using the well-established Holland interest framework. It does not measure intelligence, ability or the grades you'll get in an exam. Your results can shift as you gain experience, so retake it after a year or after a big change like starting university. Treat it as a well-informed conversation starter, and combine it with your grades, practical considerations and advice from teachers and working professionals.

faq.q: My results show two very different letters. Which one should I follow?
faq.a: You don't have to choose. Mixed codes, like Artistic with Conventional or Realistic with Social, often point to unusual and valuable careers. An A-C person might excel in architectural documentation, UX research or publishing. An R-S person might thrive in physiotherapy, emergency services or vocational teaching. Look for roles that use both sides of you, and remember that hobbies and side projects can satisfy an interest your main job doesn't.

faq.q: Should I study abroad or stay close to home?
faq.a: Your Career Compass tells you what you might enjoy, not where to study it. Weigh the costs, scholarships (Chevening, Fulbright, Commonwealth, DAAD and university awards), visa and post-study work rules, and whether your field has strong options where you already live. Professions like medicine, law and nursing have licensing rules that differ by country, so check them before you choose where to train. Many students complete a strong bachelor's close to family and move for a master's, which is often shorter, more affordable and more focused. If your family has already moved countries once, talk honestly about what another move would mean for everyone.
